#1254. 'Star Trek' star Patrick Stewart dies age 86

The Shakespearean actor landed the role of a lifetime as "Star Trek" Captain Picard. He passed away at age 86.

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!"

Stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

In the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a big deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway."

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1252. Chelsea Confidential: Meet Sebas Parrilla, the fiery, marathon-running, Bruce Springsteen fan Xabi Alonso trusts above all others - and why he's the man to fix Blues' defensive crisis

Published: 12:00 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:04 EST, 25 November 2026

Xabi Alonso is not alone in trying to halt Chelsea’s lurch into crisis. He is surrounded by a small army of staff. Some may be familiar to you, others less so.

There is Willie Isa, the ‘cultural architect’ preparing the defenders for headed duels by acting as a human shield in training drills.

There is Andre Reis, the new set-piece analyst studying Nottingham Forest’s approach to corners so Austin MacPhee can formulate instructions for the team.

There is Simon Morris and Stu Sullivan, the sports massage therapists preparing the players for their Friday night turnaround. And so on.

But the voice Alonso trusts most at Chelsea belongs to Sebastian Parrilla Simione, better known as ‘Sebas’.

The little-known Argentinian, a 49-year-old with a UEFA Pro Licence and love of marathon running and Bruce Springsteen, is his closest confidant and has been by his side ever since they oversaw an unbeaten season for Real Madrid’s Under 14s in 2018-19.

Xabi Alonso's most trusted lieutenant is Sebastian 'Sebas' Parrilla, a 49-year-old Bruce Springsteen fan with a tendency to get fired up on the touchline

Alonso had asked for an experienced aide to assist him at Real, and he was handed Parrilla, who was born in Argentina, raised in Spain, and despite not playing professionally had worked for Madrid’s academy since 2002. Parrilla coached all age ranges, from the Under 11s to the B team.

He had Alonso’s ear as their Under 14s won all but one game, and their bond was strong enough that Parrilla ended his 17-year association with Madrid’s academy when he accompanied his manager to Real Sociedad B in 2019. Then he followed him to Bayer Leverkusen in 2022, back to Real Madrid in 2025, and now Chelsea.

There is a little fire to Parrilla. He is already one caution away from a touchline suspension, having been booked against Tottenham Hotspur and Everton. While the analytical Parrilla prefers a low profile, he is Alonso’s alter ego.

The English winter will not only test Parrilla’s preference for wearing shorts whatever the weather, but also Chelsea's ability to arrest their slump with games coming thick and fast – there are seven Premier League fixtures to tackle between now and 2027, starting with Forest on Friday.

One area of focus on the training field this week has been defence. Chelsea have conceded 20 goals in the Premier League, as many as they have scored. Their shakiness at the back has been their downfall of late, and Parrilla was credited with helping organise the Leverkusen back line which went unbeaten in winning the Bundesliga in 2023-24.

When Leverkusen won 5-1 away at Eintracht Frankfurt in May 2024 to maintain their Invincibles tag with two games to go, Alonso was serving a touchline ban. Parrilla manned the technical area and after full time, Granit Xhaka and Co celebrated by pouring water over him.

Parrilla was fine with that, but less pleased during the game with how they conceded a goal from a corner to Hugo Ekitike and gifted other chances to Omar Marmoush.

One source at Leverkusen that we consulted this week credited Parrilla with improving players individually and taking the lead on set-pieces.

When Leverkusen scored from one corner routine against Hoffenheim in November 2023, Parrilla was the architect. He had certain players act as barriers to stop defenders from rushing to block the ball as it was rolled to the edge of the box, where Alex Grimaldo was on hand to power home.

Chelsea have their own set-piece specialist in MacPhee, poached from Aston Villa in the summer, so Parrilla has less control over set-pieces at Cobham.

We do not yet know whether Alonso and Parrilla will decide to change Chelsea’s centre backs for Forest. Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana were bullied by Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey and Leeds United’s Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the last two losses.

Former Chelsea man Liam Delap is the next No9 to contend with, and won't be short on motivation.

There is the added complication that Fofana has conducted an unauthorised interview, released this week, in which he laughed off Chelsea's Carabao Cup exit after his penalty miss at Liverpool. Chelsea declined to comment when asked whether that would lead to any internal punishment.

Alonso and Parrilla have been joined at the hip since the former began working with Real Madrid's Under 14s in 2018

Levi Colwill was bullied by Leeds' Dominic Calvert-Lewin in Chelsea's humiliating 4-1 loss last weekend

Alonso’s options are limited. Frustrated as he will have been by his side's 4-1 loss to Leeds, he had no senior replacements for Colwill or Fofana to call on from the bench. The only substitute with 'experience' at centre back was 18-year-old Olutayo Subuloye.

Aaron Anselmino, who represented Argentina in the last international break but has not appeared for Chelsea at all this season, did not make the matchday squad.

Maxence Lacroix is still sidelined, but Alonso told us last week he hopes he will return before 2027. Josh Acheampong and Jorrel Hato could be used centrally rather than as full backs.

As well as assisting Alonso, Parrilla acted as a bridge to the academy at Leverkusen, regularly in contact with Sergi Runge when he was head coach of the Under 17s and Under 19s.

Despite the success of the first team, Parrilla never lost the love for coaching youngsters, agreeing to help the Under 8s with community sessions on occasion. Throwing in Subuloye, who was on Chelsea’s pre-season tour in the summer but has yet to appear competitively, would surely be too big of an ask.

Until better options arrive, it would seem Parrilla is having to try to work his magic in the shadows with Colwill and Fofana. Both players know they need to improve – and fast.

Chelsea have headaches on the horizon, with Alejandro Garnacho not their only loan star struggling to convince his new club of his worth.

Garnacho suffered the ultimate indignity when Aston Villa lost 1-0 to Galatasaray in the Champions League on Tuesday. Despite Unai Emery being able to name 12 substitutes in Istanbul, he took only 11 with him including two goalkeepers, and still excluded Garnacho. When asked why, Emery said: ‘The players who were here are who I think are the best players to be here with us.’

Garnacho, 22, joined Villa on a season-long loan with a £42.5million conditional obligation dependent upon making a certain number of appearances. It is still not being disclosed how many matches it would take to trigger the clause, which has been described by sources as confidential. Chelsea insiders previously claimed it was easily achievable.

Alejandro Garnacho (right) is one of several Chelsea players having a miserable time out on loan

But Garnacho has appeared only four times in the Premier League this season, and the last of those appearances was a three-minute cameo against Fulham on October 31. He has not yet started a game in any competition.

While there is no break clause in the contract, it is understood it is possible for both Villa and Chelsea to agree to terminate his loan in January. That situation is one to watch.

But Garnacho is not the only problem loanee that Chelsea might need to address in the near future.

Robert Sanchez is on a 'dry' loan at Como, meaning there is no option or obligation to buy. The 29-year-old Spaniard has started just five of 17 games in all competitions this season.

Another goalkeeper, 24-year-old Filip Jorgensen, is on loan at Chelsea’s sister side Strasbourg, who are hovering around the Ligue 1 relegation zone and have hired Vitor Matos out of Swansea to try to lift them. His is also a dry loan.

Mykhailo Mudryk is with Tottenham, where he has only played 16 minutes in total. He is now working his way back from what Roberto De Zerbi described as a ‘stupid’ ankle injury in training.

Spurs hold a lofty £75m option to buy the 25-year-old Ukrainian, who also did an ill-advised interview last week which was not approved by either Tottenham or Chelsea.

Axel Disasi, 28, is at bottom club Crystal Palace on a straightforward loan. If relegated, Disasi is unlikely to consider staying permanently, having made that clear when West Ham dropped down to the Championship last season.

Mykhailo Mudryk (right) is with Tottenham, where he has only played 16 minutes, thanks in part to an injury his boss Roberto De Zerbi described as 'stupid'

Mamadou Sarr (left) is a rare case - a Chelsea loanee who is playing regularly for his new club, Real Sociedad

Benoit Badiashile, 25, is with Napoli, who have a £23.1m option to sign him permanently if they wish but have had a disappointing start in Serie A, lying down in eighth, 14 points behind league leaders Lazio. Badiashile has started three times in the league, and is currently injured.

Mamadou Sarr is with Real Sociedad, a loan which is also believed not to contain an option to buy, but the 21-year-old has been starting regularly for them in La Liga and the Europa League.

Other loans include Dastan Satpayev, the 18-year-old Kazakh who has been given a harsh welcome to English football with Championship strugglers Burnley (and is also injured), and Caleb Wiley, 21, also in the relegation zone with Preston.

#1251. De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Peptides capable of modulating two therapeutic targets offer opportunities for treating complex diseases1,2. However, the development of such peptides at both targets is challenging, limited primarily by low design success rates and weak bioactivity. Here we present ORIDTP, an artificial intelligence platform that integrates single-target knowledge transfer and dual-target reinforcement to enable the rational design of high-potency peptides. ORIDTP successfully designed dual-target co-agonists for the GLP-1R and glucagon receptor (GCGR, also known as GLR), six of which surpassed the strongest natural binders of each receptor in bioactivity. Notably, the lead peptide GA-Dual.R5.S3 induced substantial weight loss and glycaemic improvement in diet-induced obese mice, and exhibited pronounced antidiabetic effects in db/db mice, without inducing nausea or aversion. Furthermore, ORIDTP demonstrated generalizability through successful zero-shot design of dual-target co-inhibitors for structurally and mechanistically distinct immune checkpoints, PD-1 and CTLA-4. Out of 15 designed peptides, 8 blocked both checkpoint interactions and 3 further exhibited in vivo antitumour efficacy in human checkpoint knock-in tumour-bearing mice. The lead peptide IC-Dual.P3 achieved the strongest tumour growth suppression, reducing tumour volume by 94.2% relative to controls. Together, these findings establish ORIDTP as a powerful and generalizable platform for de novo dual-target peptide discovery.

#1250. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

#1249. Leeds United Make Release Clause Change As Calvert-Lewin Signs New Contract

Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new contract with Leeds United to put a stop to speculation surrounding his future at Elland Road.

The striker had been the subject of plenty of transfer talk, with Manchester United one of the clubs firmly in the shake-up to sign him in the January transfer window.

United are looking for a striker in the winter window, with new boss Mauricio Pochettino keen to add more firepower to his front line. Benjamin Sesko is out injured, while Joshua Zirkzee does not seem to have a future at Old Trafford.

That has left Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha as the options to lead the line, leading to speculation around who could come in.

And by signing the deal, he has wiped out a clause that would have handed United a better chance of signing him in January.

GIVEMESPORT understands that the new deal for the 29-year-old removes a release clause in the old deal that could have allowed clubs to sign him this winter for below his market value. Anyone wishing to make a move to sign him now will have to pay top dollar, which is likely to rule United out.

Calvert-Lewin has enjoyed his spell with the Whites so far, having arrived on a free transfer from Everton in the summer of 2025. #1248. What's wrong with Erling Haaland? Man City's superstar has been radiating an air of gloom in front of the cameras - but it's his form on the pitch that should most concern Enzo Maresca, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 08:22 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:10 EST, 25 November 2026

A smile did eventually spread across the face of Erling Haaland when dissecting Manchester City’s draw with Napoli, stretching their worrying run to one victory in five games.

Not for the first time in recent weeks, he had appeared morose and despondent, radiating an air of gloom, talking about how the team are ‘questioning anything’ amid these results. That’s not exactly inspiring confidence among their supporters.

But just as City’s captain for the night was about to finish his media duties before heading home, one final question focused on Sunday’s clash with Arsenal and a rivalry with a ‘certain centre half’. Haaland’s mood changed instantly.

‘It's always good to play against the best teams,’ said the Norwegian, breaking out into a smirk as he allowed the impending battle with Gabriel to percolate.

‘Arsenal were the best team last year and one of the best in the last five years now, so it's fun to play against them and it’s always fun to play against Gabriel.’

There was, at last, some positive emotion. Is Gabriel and that playground scrapping what he needs to re-energise? We’ll find out in a few days.

Erling Haaland appeared morose and despondent following Man City's draw with Napoli, suggesting he was 'questioning everything' amid their worrying run of form

Haaland did raise a smile about the prospect of his impending battle with Arsenal defender Gabriel this weekend

The Man City star has shown increasing dejected body language during games and has spent too much time recently with his head bowed and hand waving at team-mates

Haaland talked about City needing to be at their maximum to take anything from the Emirates this weekend. Whether that is ‘fun’ or not is a different matter entirely, but what Enzo Maresca must demand more from all of his players. Even with 14 goals already this term, that includes Haaland.

He is leading from the front off the pitch. Standing in front of the cameras more than anyone else, facing up to the dipping form and taking on those responsibilities without complaining. The forward wrote on X on Wednesday afternoon: 'Together through the ups and downs. Thank you for pushing us until the very end yesterday. Full focus on Sunday now.'

Yet City need more of that leadership between the white lines from somebody who has drawn a blank in four of his last five club matches, despite scoring three times over the international break.

There is too much head bowing and hand waving at the moment.

The 26-year-old admits he has to give extra. And believes that the team are generally creating enough chances for him, even if the freewheeling attacking abandon of early season has vanished.

City's results are clearly affecting Haaland’s mood and that can be self-perpetuating. He admits that failing to reverse this run is hurting him. That is evident by watching his increasingly dejected body language during games and the frustration seen when he gestured at Abdukodir Khusanov as the defender dithered with a routine throw-in during Saturday’s draw against Fulham. It wasn’t the picture of a man happy with his lot.

Only Haaland will know whether that general angst is contributing to a lack of intensity in his own performances. Nobody has mentioned the striker carrying a knock, although Maresca has appeared focused on offering him rest whenever possible over the past three months.

Something is undoubtedly proving an obstacle for him. He’s insisted that it isn’t the guilty verdicts hanging over City and, listening to him, the gripes and disappointment look focused on City’s lack of control in games. It also cannot help that Haaland will feel aggrieved to have seen a goal on Saturday chalked off for a foul on Bernd Leno and then to have not been awarded a penalty for grappling on Tuesday night.

If both or even one of those decisions go his way, the interview that sparked concern with fans – one conducted almost immediately after full time when emotions are at their highest – would likely have been very different.

City will have to cling on to the idea that a sullen Haaland is at least a Haaland who cares. And a Haaland who cares must surely dig them out of this hole, even if he cannot do that alone.

#1247. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

#1246. Carlo Ancelotti Named 5 Best Players He's Ever Coached

Carlo Ancelotti once offered insight into his approach to managing players, explaining that footballers are human beings rather than machines and deserve to be treated accordingly. The legendary Italian explained that his players should see themselves as men who happen to play football, rather than simply footballers.

It is a philosophy that every aspiring football manager would benefit from adopting, particularly given Ancelotti's standing among the best managers in world football. His record in the Champions League is unmatched, having become the first and only manager to lift the trophy five times.

Five is also a fitting number for 'Don Carlo', who remains the only manager to have won league titles in all five of Europe's major domestic competitions. Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and Bayern Munich have all experienced life with the Italian in charge.

Throughout his managerial career, Ancelotti has worked alongside some truly exceptional footballers. But which five players stand above the rest in his estimation? He revealed his selections in November 2022.

Carlo Ancelotti faced a number of managers in his career but one name sticks out more than others

Ronaldo Nazario was no longer at the height of his powers when he joined AC Milan in January 2007, with persistent injuries having already taken their toll on the Brazilian forward. In his prime, Brazil's legendary number nine was virtually impossible to stop, while his displays at the 2002 World Cup remain among the finest individual efforts in tournament history.

Ancelotti was managing Milan when the 30-year-old striker arrived in northern Italy for what was effectively the closing chapter of his European career. Although Ronaldo was past his best, he still showed flashes of the extraordinary ability that had made him one of football's greatest-ever forwards.

"We signed Ronaldo when I was at Milan. He weighed 220 lbs. Before a match I said to him: 'You have to lose weight'. He replied: 'What do you want me to do? If you want me to run, put me on the bench, if you want me to score, play with me'! I played with him and he didn't run, but he scored two goals" (via Soccer Addict).

GIVEMESPORT Key Fact: Ronaldo Nazario could not feature in AC Milan's 2006-07 Champions League-winning campaign, having already represented Real Madrid in the competition.

Ancelotti once revealed that he would have enjoyed the opportunity to coach Lionel Messi, but only as a way of comparing him with Cristiano Ronaldo. His comments make it clear that the former Real Madrid boss holds the Portuguese superstar in exceptionally high regard when discussing football's greatest players.

Cristiano Ronaldo spent two campaigns working under Ancelotti at the Santiago Bernabeu, a partnership that delivered remarkable results. The Italian's supportive, almost fatherly management style is reminiscent of Sir Alex Ferguson, Ronaldo's former Manchester United manager. Ancelotti places considerable importance on creating a close-knit environment, something that helped the prolific forward flourish.

Ancelotti's first spell in Madrid also saw the emergence of one of the most devastating attacking combinations in the club's history. Cristiano Ronaldo, Karim Benzema and Gareth Bale formed the famous trio, with Ronaldo collecting two Ballons d'Or during that period.

"Ronaldo is a great talent physically and technically, it's his nature... And he complemented these characteristics with unique seriousness and professionalism. I've never seen a player so attentive, prepared, concentrated, focused. He's a model for others, certainly, in terms of preparation" (via GOAL).

Champions League, Copa del Rey, UEFA Super Cup, FIFA Club World Cup

Zlatan Ibrahimovic worked with Ancelotti for only one season, yet their time together proved hugely productive. The Swedish striker was instrumental in an exciting period of growth for Paris Saint-Germain as the club began its transformation following the Qatar Sports Investments takeover in 2011.

Ancelotti took charge in January 2012, with Ibrahimovic arriving as the marquee addition to help establish PSG as a major force in European football. Having previously crossed paths at AC Milan, the two already shared some history, and the striker enjoyed an outstanding spell in the French capital.

Their relationship remained strong long after their time in Paris, with speculation emerging in 2019 that the pair could work together again at Everton. Ibrahimovic ultimately never made the move to Goodison Park, although reports in Italy suggested Ancelotti had made an effort to bring his former player to Merseyside.

“Behind this mask of arrogance there is a great professional and a great altruist. Zlatan was one of the few players I coached who took more pleasure in providing an assist than scoring a goal, in Paris it was like that. He is a great player and a great character" (via Football Italia).

Every manager has certain players with whom they develop an almost perfect working relationship. Ancelotti has enjoyed partnerships with several legendary footballers, but his connection with Karim Benzema stands out as particularly special, both professionally and personally.

The bond between the French striker and his former Real Madrid manager was evident throughout their two spells together. During their first period at the club, Benzema was a key component of the famous 'BBC' attack. Their second stint together, however, produced memories that Madrid supporters will treasure for years to come.

Benzema eventually developed into the team's leading figure, taking on the captaincy and establishing himself among Europe's elite. His performances throughout the 2021-22 Champions League campaign were extraordinary, and Ancelotti was perfectly placed to appreciate just how special his striker had become.

"I have coached one of the best players in football history, a complete forward, a very friendly, humble, and serious person" (via The Athletic).

"He is really complete, not just as a striker but as a player. Benzema scores a lot of goals and this is really important but he also helps the team a lot in possession" (via Reuters).

Champions League x2, La Liga, Copa del Rey x2, Supercopa de Espana, UEFA Super Cup x2, FIFA Club World Cup x2

Vinicius Junior's development under Ancelotti was remarkable. The Brazilian evolved into one of the best wingers in the world, improving both his technical ability and understanding of the game under the Italian's guidance. Ancelotti was among those who repeatedly backed him to claim the Ballon d'Or before the controversy surrounding the award in October 2024.

Across four seasons together in Spain, Vinicius matured into the elite performer supporters see today, and he has regularly acknowledged Ancelotti's influence on his progress. His respect for the manager was clear, with the winger even expressing a desire to see him coach both Real Madrid and Brazil – a wish that later came true.

Although the Ballon d'Or ultimately eluded Vinicius in one of the award's biggest controversies, his performances during Ancelotti's second spell in Madrid were outstanding. The trust and attacking freedom given to him after his breakthrough into the senior side helped turn him into a central figure in the club's Champions League and La Liga successes.

"When I arrived [at Real Madrid in 2021], I'd only seen him on TV. I got here and I found a player with a spectacular talent. Around that talent, he's been able to add a lot of things: the ability to lose his marker, more efficiency in front of goal. He's done it with a spectacular daily work ethic, always very focused in training" (via ESPN).

Vinicius Junior under Carlo Ancelotti (at Real Madrid)

Champions League x2, La Liga, Copa del Rey, Supercopa de Espana x2, UEFA Super Cup, FIFA Club World Cup x2

The Real Madrid boss is the king of the Champions League.

#1245. Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 979–986 (2026) Cite this article

Modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering. To circumvent this unwanted behaviour, here, we explore the fundamental limits of charge transport in topological semimetal niobium phosphide (NbP) nanoribbons down to approximately 6-nm widths, with industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication. The extracted NbP nanoribbon resistivity reaches 18 ± 4.1 μΩ cm at room temperature with an approximately 9-nm2 cross-sectional area, lower than that of conventional metals and semimetals with comparable size. The NbP nanoribbon resistivity decreases with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper. This trend suggests a growing relative contribution of surface and edge states as the nanoribbon cross-section is reduced, despite a certain amount of disorder, including edge roughness. Our findings advance the understanding of size-dependent transport and scaling in this class of semimetals, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects in future nanoelectronics.

a, High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) image of the NbP (1.5 nm) nanoribbon with Nb (3.4 nm) seed layer. The electrically-conducting width of this device is ~12.5 nm. b, Magnified view of the nanocrystalline NbP layer and crystalline Nb seed, together with their corresponding Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), obtained from the boxed regions in panel a. c,d, Bright-field image (c) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental map (d) of the same device, showing distinct material compositions. In total, three NbP (1.5 nm) nanoribbons were examined by cross-sectional STEM. Across these samples, we observe consistent structural and compositional characteristics, including similar NbP crystallinity and sidewall oxidation, which support the scaling behaviour reported in this work. Additional STEM characterization was not performed on thicker NbP nanoribbons, as the thinnest nanoribbons are most relevant to the main conclusions of this study.

a, HAADF image of the NbP (1.5 nm)/Nb (3.4 nm) nanoribbon with an electrically-conducting width of ~18 nm. b, Magnified view of the nanocrystalline NbP layer and crystalline Nb seed layer, together with their corresponding FFT, obtained from the boxed regions. c,d, Bright-field image (c) and EDS elemental map (d) of the same device, showing distinct material compositions of each region. e, EELS linescan profiles of Nb (blue) and P (red) normalized intensity as a function of position along the direction indicated in panel c. f-h, Representative nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED) patterns extracted from 4D-STEM data at probe positions within the sapphire substrate (f), Nb layer (g), and NbP layer (h), with indexed reflections confirming the distinct crystal structure of each region. i-k, Orientation template matching of the representative NBED pattern in f–h, for the sapphire substrate (i), Nb layer (j) and NbP layer (k). Coloured symbols indicate the local crystallographic orientation of the best-matching template for that pattern. l-n, Phase template matching of the same patterns for the sapphire substrate (l), Nb layer (m) and NbP layer (n).

a, Schematic of the scaling mechanism for conventional metals, with surface scattering and grain boundary scattering. b, As thickness and width of NbP are reduced, the conduction is consistent with the growing dominance of surface carriers, which are disorder-tolerant, with reduced scattering. The total sheet conductance in this case is a sum of the sheet conductance contributed from bulk carriers and surface carriers. c, For thick NbP, bulk carriers dominate the transport, and thus conventional scaling laws apply, with pronounced surface and grain boundary scattering. d, The Fuchs-Sondheimer (FS) and Mayadas-Shatzkes (MS) model fitting of 3.4 nm Nb seed layer, showing an excellent fit. The extracted resistivity with increasing width (W → ∞) is 56.3 μΩ∙cm, which matches the literature results. e, Sheet conductance (GNbP,□) of 1.5 nm NbP as a function of width (red curve), extracted from Fig. 2d of the main text. The sheet conductance from bulk carriers (extracted from Hall measurement) follows the conventional FS-MS scaling model (black dashed line), where the sheet conductance from surface carriers increases as the width decreases due to the increased surface area/volume ratio, as indicated by the purple dashed line. At this ultrathin thickness (1.5 nm), bulk carriers experience strong scattering, resulting in very small bulk carrier sheet conductance. f, GNbP,□ of 10 nm NbP as a function of width (blue curve). At NbP thickness of 10 nm, 3D bulk carriers and 2D top and bottom surface carriers contribute comparably to transport, as shown in Fig. 4b. At this thickness, as the nanoribbon width is reduced, the enhancement in surface conduction is insufficient to offset the increased scattering of bulk carriers. Consequently, bulk transport dominates in this regime, leading to a net reduction of sheet conductance (i.e., increased resistivity) with decreasing width, more similar to conventional metal wires. We note that there could be subtle differences in sidewall roughness and damage in the thicker nanoribbons compared to the thinner ones. See Supplementary Note 2 for the modelling details and more discussion.

a, Bulk Brillouin-zone schematic showing the two mirror planes and nodal rings from the band inversion. b, Representative band dispersion along Γ-S-M’, where the curves calculated without spin-orbit coupling (SOC) show the nodal-ring-related band inversion (plotted in green), and the curves calculated with SOC show the corresponding gap opening (black dashed lines). c, Real-space crystal view highlighting the helical states along the projected mirror line on the surface. d, Surface-state spectrum along \(\overline{\Gamma }\)-\(\overline{{\rm{X}}}\)-\(\overline{\Gamma }\)’, where the narrow Weyl-point window (grey shadow) hosts three pairs of helical states (indicated by arrows) that form the main part of the Fermi arcs, while remnant spin-split surface branches remain visible over a broader energy window (broad green shadow). Blue and red colours indicate the ‘± Sy’ spin polarization at opposite momenta, showing the helical feature. In summary, the narrow Fermi-arc structure is embedded inside a much broader nodal-ring-derived surface-state sector set by the band inversion. See Supplementary Note 7 for more discussion on bulk-topology hierarchy and topological surface-state interpretation.

a, Slab model along the [001] direction for the surface state calculations. Here, the 2 × 2 × 3 supercell is shown as an example. A 4.5 nm thick slab structure of the 1 × 1 × 4 supercell was used in the calculations. b,c, Surface band structures with Nb (b) and P (c) terminations along high-symmetry lines. Blue and red bands indicate the surface states of the Nb and P terminations, respectively. Bulk-projected states shown in pale blue are depicted as the background. The charge neutral point is set to 0 eV. d-f, Surface-projected Fermi surfaces with Nb (upper panels) and P (lower panels) terminations at 0 eV (d), −0.2 eV (e), and −0.4 eV (f). Darker colours represent larger contributions projected from the surface. Weyl points projected on the 2D Brillouin zone are shown as green and purple dots for opposite chirality. The constant energy cuts show surface-dominant open contours over a broad energy window, indicating that Weyl-derived surface bands persist even when the chemical potential is shifted deep into the hole-doped regime, which implies the robustness of the topological surface character. In addition, for the 4.5 nm thick NbP film, the top and bottom surface states exhibit minimal hybridization, except near the Weyl point projections where they meet each other. The Fermi-arc states remain largely unhybridized because they are well separated in momentum space. Even at momenta where they intersect, the resulting hybridization gap is negligible. See Supplementary Note 8 for the modelling details and more discussion.

a, Slab model from the NbP (001) film with thickness d = 1.5 nm and width W = 4.4 to 5.7 nm. b, The one-dimensional (1D) band structure of a W = 5 nm nanoribbon along ky direction. The edge projection is highlighted in purple to show the edge states, while the bulk states are shown in pale blue. Near EF, the edge-projected subbands form an electron-like pocket, consistent with the negative pedge values (panel f). c-e, The spin projection to Sx (c), Sy (d), and Sz (e) components, respectively, for the edge state. The blue and red represent opposite signs of spin polarization. These edge states exhibit a pronounced spin texture arising from strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in noncentrosymmetric NbP where Sx and Sz components are locked to the ky momentum in a Rashba-type SOC. This reduces the wavefunction overlap between counter-propagating modes, thereby suppressing the leading backscattering channel, which indicates high-mobility edge conduction. f, The carrier densities from edge (pedge) and 2D film (p2D) are extracted from linear fitting of the total ribbon density (p1D) by p1D = pedge + p2DW, at varying W. Wc denotes the cross-over width at which the edge carrier density would dominate the transport over the top and bottom surface carrier density. Here, Wc ≈ 0 indicates that the enhanced edge conduction of ultrathin films is not primarily driven by an increased edge carrier density. Instead, it is more plausibly attributed to an enhanced carrier mobility arising from reduced backscattering as the edge dimension approaches the quasi-1D limit. See more details in Supplementary Notes 2 and 8. g, Agreement between the nanoribbon fitting (\({p}_{2{\rm{D}}}^{{\rm{NR}}}\)) and that obtained from independent slab film calculations (\({p}_{2{\rm{D}}}^{{\rm{slab}}}\)) which corresponds to the d = 1.5 nm thickness in Supplementary Fig. 10. This agreement supports the self-consistency of our calculations across both the nanoribbon and thin-film geometries.

a, Temperature-dependent effective resistivity (ρeff) of NbP films with different thicknesses up to 90 nm, measured from Hall bar devices. These films have a 3.4 nm Nb seed layer, whose resistivity is measured separately (black symbols). b, Low-temperature limit (2-10 K) of panel a. The smallest superconducting transition temperature Tc (~2.2 K) is in the 3.4 nm Nb layer (black symbols), while higher Tc are observed in the NbP/Nb films, and Tc decreases monotonically with thicker NbP. The symbol colours follow the convention in panel a. c,d, Temperature-dependent sheet conductance (GNbP,□) (c) and resistivity (ρNbP) (d) for all NbP thicknesses, after subtracting the Nb seed contribution. e, ρNbP as a function of NbP thickness at 300 K and 10 K. For comparison, the ρNbP values of nanoribbons with the widest widths (Fig. 2d of the main text) are slightly higher than those from Hall measurements at 300 K, possibly due to process-induced damage during nanofabrication. f, Temperature-dependent ρeff of a ~5 nm-thick Nb control film, measured from a Hall bar device. The residual resistivity ratio (RRR) is 1.48, and the Tc is ~4.2 K. Inset: enlarged view of the low-temperature region. The presence of NbP appears to promote superconductivity in NbP/Nb films. The superconducting proximity effect is one plausible interpretation, although changes in disorder and enhanced inter-grain coupling (in the presence of NbP layer) could also contribute. We also cannot fully rule out the formation of an interfacial superconducting layer at the NbP/Nb interface. The NbP sheet conductance is obtained by subtracting the sheet conductance of the Nb layer (measured independently on control Nb films) from the total sheet conductance of the NbP/Nb stack. The extracted NbP resistivity is then obtained by dividing the NbP thickness by the NbP sheet conductance, i.e. ρNbP = dNbP/GNbP,□, where GNbP,□ = Gtot,□ - GNb,□ and Gtot,□ = dtot/ρeff, where Gtot,□ is the total sheet conductance of the NbP/Nb stack, dtot is the total stack thickness and ρeff is the measured effective resistivity (panel a). The GNbP,□ (panel c) represents the NbP sheet conductance after subtracting the independently-measured Nb seed contribution. Additional validation of the subtraction method using Pt/Nb stacks is provided in Supplementary Fig. 19. Control experiments using Pt/Nb stacks validate that the subtraction procedure itself does not generate an anomalous resistivity trend. Nevertheless, the conductance of the Nb seed layer within NbP/Nb stacks cannot be independently measured and it cannot be said, with absolute certainty, that its behaviour is identical to that of the separately measured Nb control film. Thus, the extracted NbP resistivity relies, by necessity, on the model used.

a-c, Hall resistance (Rxy) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at various temperatures for 3.4 nm Nb (a), 1.5 nm NbP (b), and 10 nm NbP (c). For the NbP films (b,c), the Nb seed layer contribution is subtracted at each corresponding temperature to extract NbP Hall response, using the same two-layer Hall conduction model described in the supplement. d, Effective three-dimensional carrier density (p3D) for all films, revealing opposite temperature-dependence: ultrathin 1.5 nm NbP shows an increasing p3D upon cooling, whereas both thicker NbP (10 nm) and Nb (3.4 nm) display decreasing p3D. (This figure is also included in the main text as Fig. 4d and is reproduced here for convenience). e, Effective hole mobility (μp) of the same films vs. temperature. NbP films exhibit a pronounced increase in mobility upon cooling due to suppressed phonon scattering, whereas the 3.4 nm Nb film shows only a slight rise in mobility, indicating that its transport remains strongly limited by surface scattering.

a-c, Longitudinal sheet resistance (Rxx) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at various temperatures for films of Nb seed layer (3.4 nm) (a), for NbP (1.5 nm) on the Nb seed (b), and for NbP (10 nm) on the Nb seed (c). All measurements were performed with the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the film plane and current direction. At low temperatures, all films exhibit a pronounced negative cusp near low field regions, arising from the interplay of superconducting fluctuations and weak antilocalization. d-e, Longitudinal sheet resistance (Rxx) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at 1.8 K for both 1.5 nm thick NbP (on 3.4 nm Nb seed layer) and for the Nb layer (3.4 nm) evaluated separately. Measurements were performed with B field perpendicular to the film plane and current direction (d), and with B applied in-plane (e). The superconducting transition temperatures are Tc ~ 6 K for the 1.5 nm NbP (on Nb) and ~2.2 K for the 3.4 nm Nb film (see Fig. 3d of the main text). The upper critical field Hc2, defined as the midpoint between the normal state resistance and zero resistance, is extracted. At 1.8 K, the out-of-plane critical field \({H}_{c2}^{\perp }\) is 2.2 T for NbP (1.5 nm) and 0.38 T for Nb (3.4 nm). The in-plane critical field at 1.8 K exceeds 9 T for NbP (1.5 nm) and reaches 4.44 T for Nb (3.4 nm). The superconducting coherence length estimates are provided in the supplement. The sense current used for Hall bar measurements is 0.5 mA, corresponding to a current density of ~0.1 MA/cm2 for the NbP (1.5 nm) film and ~0.15 MA/cm2 for the 3.4 nm Nb control, with the same 100 μm Hall bar device width. We note that this sense current is well below the superconducting critical current: even when we increased the sense current up to 10 mA, we were unable to suppress the superconducting state at 1.8 K.

a, Cross-sectional HAADF STEM image of the alternating NbP/Nb multilayers grown on sapphire. b-d, Denoised nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED) patterns extracted from 4D-STEM data for all Nb layers (Nb layers 1-3) showing consistent body-centred cubic (bcc) diffraction symmetry with indexed reflections, confirming crystalline quality across all Nb layers. Scale bars: 0.5 Å−1. e, EDS line scan across the multilayer stack showing Nb (blue), P (red), and Al (light brown) as a function of position, integrated over a ~ 5nm wide region along the direction indicated by the yellow arrow in panel a, confirming periodic composition and abrupt elemental transitions at each NbP/Nb interface. f-h, denoised NBED patterns from NbP layers 1–3, displaying diffraction symmetry consistent with the NbP crystal structure with indexed reflections, consistent with uniform phase and crystallographic orientation throughout the multilayer stack. The diffraction spots become progressively broader from layer 1 to layer 3, suggesting a gradual decrease in crystalline coherence in NbP layers further from the substrate. This is further supported by the emergence of diffuse ring features in the Layer 3 diffraction pattern, indicative of increasing structural disorder.

#1244. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

#1243. Larin or Lankshear: Better Striker Named Before Southampton vs Middlesbrough

Southampton and Middlesbrough meet for the first time since the final Spygate verdict at St Mary's on Friday night, with former Saints Billy Sharp exclusively telling GIVEMESPORT which club has the better striker.

Southampton and their manager Tonda Eckert were found guilty of spying on three Championship opponents last season, including Boro ahead of their Championship playoff semi-final first leg, which saw them expelled from the final against Hull City at Wembley.

Saints had beaten the Teesside outfit over two legs to reach one of the most lucrative finals in football, but they were thrown out just days before the fixture.

Kim Hellberg's side were reinstated but were unable to take advantage, losing 1-0 to the Tigers in the final, to ensure they remained in the Championship for another season.

As well as their expulsion, the south coast outfit were also given a minus-four points deduction to start the 2026-27 campaign, which they did quickly overcome.

Southampton and Middlesbrough have quickly proved they are two of the best teams in the division, with the former top of the table after 17 matches with 35 points.

Saints would be in fourth with 32 points without the deduction, but instead they are sixth and their away from continues to let them down.

Eckert's men have taken 22 points from a possible 24 at home this term, with only Boro bettering that tally (23), although they have played once more at the Riverside Stadium.

While a lot of focus will be on the Eckert vs Hellberg rivalry on what is sure to be an electric atmosphere at St Mary's, a lot of eyes will also be on Cyle Larin and Will Lankshear.

They are considered by many to be the two best number nines in the league, with Larin scoring every 103 minutes this season, while Lankshear has netted every 80 minutes for Boro.

Both have had their injury issues, with Larin missing four games in total and Lankshear two, but both are fit and available for Friday night.

While both players have their strengths, Billy Sharp has revealed in an exclusive with GMS who he believes the 'better' centre-forward is.

Speaking to GIVEMESPORT exclusively, the recently-retired striker said: “Two good players. I do like Cyle Larin. His movement is good, he’s a big, strong boy. He had a good World Cup.

"He's been struggling with an injury, and I think that’s the thing. I felt as though I was robust and that’s why I scored a lot of goals in the Championship and the EFL, because I could churn out the games. Cyle Larin has had a few niggles this season, Lankshear has struggled with a hamstring injury. When your team relies on you to play week in, week out, Saturday, Tuesday, it is hard, and you’ve got to keep yourself fit.

“It’s a shame that both of them can’t stay fit, because I did say at the start of the season that those two, and Jarrod Bowen, would be up there with the top scorers.

I loved being the one to score the goals and get the team as high as you can, and I’m sure Will Lankshear and Cyle Larin do as well. But both good strikers. I’d probably just say Will Lankshear is better.

It's hard to disagree with Sharp, based on what we've seen this season.

Larin is clearly a brilliant striker at this level who has proven he is vital to Southampton and their style of play, but you simply can't argue with Lankshear's numbers this season.

14 goals in 15 Championship appearances is a remarkable number, and the 21-year-old looks as though he will score every time he plays.

It will be interesting to see the two face off against each other on Friday, and who comes out on top in a match where both sides would lay down a huge marker with victory.

Billy Sharp was speaking at the launch of the Panini EFL 2026/27 Official Sticker Collection in London. The collection is available now at retailers nationwide and online via Panini.co.uk.
