#1191. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

#1190. U17 World Cup: Italy maintain perfect record with 3-1 victory

Italy maintained their 100 per cent record in the FIFA Under-17 World Cup, winning all three group games to secure top spot and passage to the Round of 32.

The Azzurrini had already thumped Jamaica 6-0 and saw off the Ivory Coast 2-1, then this afternoon got the better of Uzbekistan 3-1.

It sees them top Group E with nine points out of nine, guaranteeing access to the Round of 32.

However, Riccardo Cassano will not participate in that fixture because he was sent off for two bookable offences, and will therefore be suspended.

Tommaso Casagrande, Federico Croci and Thomas Corigliano had the result all sewn up before half-time, with Sukhrob Sadirjanov netting a consolation for Uzbekistan.

Italy are among the favourites to win the tournament in Qatar, having already won the European Under-17 Championship under coach Daniele Franceschini.

The Azzurrini will find out the names of their next opponents on Friday, to see which are the best third-place finishers.

#1189. Senne Lammens has NOT fully recovered from World Cup howler, claims Peter Schmeichel after Man United goalkeeper's nightmare in Lisbon - as Joshua Zirkzee insists squad will rally around under-fire team-mate

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER

Published: 04:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 06:54 EST, 26 November 2026

Manchester United legend Peter Schmeichel fears Senne Lammens has yet to recover from the blunder he made during Belgium's World Cup campaign last summer.

Lammens made two costly mistakes in United’s 2-2 Champions League draw with Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday night, conceding a needless penalty and dropping a clanger in the dying minutes to allow Luis Suarez to score twice for the home side.

The 24-year-old goalkeeper, who was one of Manchester United's standout performers last season following his £18.1million transfer from Royal Antwerp, has looked unconvincing so far this term and played a part in the club conceding more goals (35) than any other side in Europe's top five leagues.

Former Red Devils goalkeeper Schmeichel believes Lammens has never fully recovered from his error that led to Belgium being dumped out by Spain at the World Cup quarter-final stage last summer.

In the 88th minute of the match, with the score locked at 1-1, Lammens spilled the ball into the path of Mikel Merino, who tapped home to send Spain through to the semi-finals.

Asked if the confidence-shot goalkeeper should now be dropped by Mauricio Pochettino for Karl Darlow, who was signed by United in the summer, Schmeichel told CBS Sports: ‘I don’t know where that point is.

Senne Lammens made two big errors during Manchester United's 2-2 draw at Sporting Lisbon

Peter Schmeichel fears Lammens has never fully recovered from his blunder at the World Cup

‘Mauricio Pochettino has come in, he’s brought his own staff, that means he’s got a new goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.

‘I don’t know if you remember in the World Cup, he came against Spain and made a bit of a mistake, Merino scored and they got knocked out, and I feel like he’s lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake, hasn’t really recovered.

‘As a goalkeeper when you’re not on your best form you need your defenders in front of you to help you out and the sad truth is that they haven’t been able to do that and of course, that makes it so much worse.'

Joshua Zirkzee insists United’s players will rally around Lammens and won’t let their under-fire goalkeeper ‘suffer by himself’.

The two costly errors undid Lammens’ good work after he saved an earlier penalty from Suarez, but Zirkzee said the players are determined to support the Belgian.

‘This team is a family, so there's no one who will suffer by themselves,’ said Zirkzee. ‘Mistakes happen. Let's go on to the next one. Senne’s a great goalkeeper.

‘In this moment, we just give him space. I’m not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne’s a great kid. He's got a good head on him and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game. We didn't draw because of him. I'm also someone who likes to look at myself and, you know, I didn't score.’

United had two goals disallowed by Polish referee Szymon Marciniak as well as conceding the two penalties and seeing Youri Tielemans sent off – three days after Leny Yoro was shown a controversial red card at Liverpool – and Zirkzee admitted that it feels like the world is against Pochettino’s team at the moment.

The Belgian shot-stopper conceded a needless penalty just minutes after saving a spot-kick

He then spilled the ball into the path of Luis Suarez late on, gifting Sporting a late equaliser

‘Yeah, we're in a place where it can feel like that pretty quick,’ he added. ‘But as I said, we've got a locker-room that's built on supporting each other and we will get out of it eventually. If it's us against the world, so be it.

‘For the team that we are, we shouldn't really be looking at what the referee decides, but you cannot deny that it was some key decisions that weren't in our favour, to put it like that.

‘But, as I said, we shouldn't really be looking at the referee. All we have to do is look at ourselves. In the end, I think we drew because of small details, little mistakes. But we definitely have something to build on, mainly the way we started the second half. I think that's something we can build on and move on with. Our team should be capable to win even if we're not being favoured in those moments.’

#1188. Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Polysaccharides have myriad functions throughout biological processes, yet synthetic access to well-defined analogues remains a challenge1,2. Achieving high molecular weight, controlled stereochemistry and sequence precision simultaneously has been elusive using conventional chemical methods that rely on protecting-group manipulations. Here we propose enzymatic living polymerization, which enables the precision preparation of natural polysaccharides with molecular weights up to 660 kg mol−1 but polydispersity from low to less than 1.05. Such a living behaviour originates from the initiator weakly binding with the polymerase, realizing fast equilibrium of the active (bound) and dormant (unbound) species, as demonstrated by mechanistic and computational studies. Our approach is generalizable to diverse polysaccharide types, including sequence-controlled block copolymers, and provides a modular route to explore molecular-weight-dependent biological functions of natural polysaccharides.

#1187. Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and said “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

FLEETWOOD TAKE THE LEAD! 😱 Loupalo-Bi puts League Two side Fleetwood ahead against Arsenal 💥 https://t.co/zTFEkCp0oL

As the home fans set off flares, filling the air with plumes of thick, red smoke, the theme tune to Captain Pugwash was played. Arteta tried to find answers from his coaching staff, amid the cacophony, but occasionally you do not have to look too deep for answers.

Could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

So it proved. Odegaard, with his mesmerising left foot and all-encompassing vision, did more in the first five minutes of the second period than many of his colleagues had managed before the interval, and Arsenal levelled in that initial flurry through Gyökeres’s first domestic goal of the campaign.

Viktor Gyökeres gets his first goal of the season and Arsenal are level against Fleetwood! 🔴 https://t.co/LfZcIbAfCX

A game of attack against defence played out for the remainder before Dowman was harshly dismissed in the 85th minute after reacting to a tough challenge from Neal. There was still time for Fleetwood’s Lynch to make two excellent saves from White and Odegaard in added time as Arsenal tried to avoid the shoot-out lottery. They could not and how it hurt them.

HUGE save from Jay Lynch! https://t.co/dLJaFwCmHQ

“Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and removed,” Matt Lawlor, the Fleetwood manager, said. “To me, there was that feeling we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special.

“To be giving that to football fans and especially Fleetwood fans is unbelievably special. I’m really proud of it. Football’s a funny old game, isn’t it?”

First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through in the next round, in the manner they’ve done it, the atmosphere they have created, and, yeah, a really sad day for us.

I cannot fault at all the attitude of the players. I haven’t seen anyone not doing what is required at this level. But, obviously, we insisted so much, we have so much of the ball, so many chances, so many shots, and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to the penalties, obviously, you need to capitalise on that. And we didn’t. And football is about that.

Attitude wise, absolutely zero [wrong] otherwise, I would be here absolutely fuming. I’m sad, I think we are all sad. We have a massive responsibility to carry this badge in the best possible way. It had nothing to do with effort or application or determination to win it, but we lack other things to, to create a much bigger margin than today, with what we produce, they really should have been shown in the scoreline.

Something that we discussed already before the match.

It’s difficult to see on the cameras, I prefer to watch it back properly and I will assess the situation.

We will learn from everything [on if he will learn from it].

I don’t think it will [sink in], it’s really hard to address the players when we have a league game on Saturday and I didn’t want to be the bearer of reality. The biggest night in the club’s history. We’ve beaten the champions, somehow!

We knew before the game, we’re not stupid enough and not egotistical enough that you think we’re going to go to the best team in the country and the most organised team in the country and the best of the basics and the world-class players, in that we’re going to go and outplay them. So we had to ride our luck, we had to deny space, we had to deny options for them. And I think we did that really, really well in terms of the majority of the game.

Obviously, the goal happens, but they’re going to happen; they’re so good at football. The footballers that they have, the gaps that they find and we see it every week in the Premier League.

To beat the English champions on penalties, credit to everyone one of these lads. We looked at Grimsby beating Man Utd last year. We compared it even though these are the champions. We thought ‘if we lay it all out there, let’s see what happens.

The team who are 18th in League Two have beaten the Premier League champions. Nine perfect penalties and one miss from Bruno Guimaraes.

Lynch dives to his left after the Guimaraes stutter, good save from the goalkeeper.

Arsenal are out if Haughey converts this penalty.

Cannon scores against Arsenal at Highbury. Bruno G up next.

Gyokeres finishes with power. The perfect record continues. Cannon up next for Fleetwood.

Meslier dives the wrong way again, Davies does well to keep his composure after needing a few attempts to spot the ball.

All four penalties have been scored, Havertz sends Lynch the wrong way after missing a few chances in regulation time.

Cracking penalty from midfielder, into the roof of the net with power.

Lynch guessed the right way, but Odegaard found the bottom-right corner with power.

He waits for Meslier to dive and rolls the ball into the opposite corner.

Odegaard is going to take first for Arsenal.

Their striker Coughlan, on as a sub in the second half, is going to take the first penalty of the shoot-out against Meslier.

Arsenal taken to penalties by the team 18th in League Two. They finish the game with a sense of injustice after Max Dowman’s red card, but they only have themselves to blame for not putting Fleetwood to the sword in the second half. Huge defensive effort from the underdogs.

Arsenal continue to pile the pressure on even with 10 men, but Guimaraes’s cross is claimed by Lynch.

Fleetwood then go on the attack, and White makes a mess of Rooney’s cross, conceding a cheap corner.

One last chance to win the tie, but Arsenal deal with it.

Havertz then heads the ball down in a dangerous zone but no Arsenal player is there. Arsenal have had their best spell since the red card, almost playing with some anger.

Brilliant save from Lynch to deny Ben White at the back post! Stopped right on the line, just as five minutes of stoppage time are shown on the board.

Then Lynch turns behind another Odegaard shot for a corner.

HUGE save from Jay Lynch! https://t.co/dLJaFwCmHQ

Bruno Guimaraes floats in a cross that is too heavy for Ben White. Fleetwood have a free-kick which they are going to send into the mixer but Arsenal clear.

Mikel Arteta did not have much sympathy for Dowman as he walked past him, but replays suggest it was a harsh call. No VAR in play tonight. Arsenal now playing with 10 for the final minutes.

I suspect Mikel Arteta will feel a little differently about this situation when he sees a replay of what actually happened. https://t.co/tflU7nc831

The Arsenal winger reacted to a heavy challenge, and the referee has judged that he kicked out. There was very little in the incident, a slight movement of his left leg rather than a full-on swing.

RED CARD for Max Dowman! 🟥 https://t.co/wq4EvRIScm

Fleetwood’s best attacking moment of the second half! White and Mosquera got themselves in a mess before Meslier made a smothering save from Davies. Havertz heads the resulting corner clear but Eze messes up a promising Arsenal break.

Arsenal continue to hog possession around the Fleetwood box, but since both teams made their subs, the home team have started to look more comfortable again. Eze’s shot is blocked, and then he is caught offside.

Arsenal making another couple of changes: Guimaraes and Konsa replace Lewis-Skelly and Zubimendi.

For Fleetwood: Davies replaces Loupalo-Bi.

Ben White caught offside just as Arsenal were building up a head of steam in attack. “Champion of England, you’re having a laugh” is the chant from the home fans.

From that Arsenal free-kick, Havertz’s low cross goes straight into the side-netting. The German has had a bit of a stinker, Arsenal will need better at Anfield on Sunday. I’m sure Arteta would have liked to have taken off Havertz or Gyokeres by now.

Haughey wins an important tackle on Lewis-Skelly after Arsenal found the free player in the box, and from the resulting short corner Dowman’s shot is straight Lynch.

Dowman is then hacked down by Batty, who was tempted in by a heavy touch. Booking for the Fleetwood defender.

If the game finishes level, we will go straight to penalties. One or two players on both teams with heavy legs, but Arsenal surely have to turn the screw from here.

Coughlan is an in-form striker who is trying to offer Fleetwood some more intensity and pressing from the front. Despite all that Arsenal pressure, Fleetwood have not gone under since conceding the equaliser.

Havertz hesitant after Odegaard picked out his run and split the Fleetwood defence again. Neither let fly with the shot from a tight angle, nor picked out a cutback. Two changes from Fleetwood: Evans and McClean off, Coughlan and Murphy on.

And a change from Arsenal: O’Neill off, replaced by Eze. O’Neill was one of Arsenal’s brighter starters.

Bodies on the line from Fleetwood to keep the scores level, first Havertz and then Lewis Skelly had shots blocked from a free-kick floated into the box. Fleetwood need to hope for a second wind from somewhere.

Odegaard with another delightful flicked pass, but Havertz could only poke the ball into the side netting. Should be doing better with that chance, he had half of the goal to aim at. Arsenal knocking on the door, feels like a second goal is coming.

Havertz’s rebound actually flicked off Bennett’s head, or else that was a certain goal. As you would expect, Fleetwood now finding it very difficult to get out of their half or establish any possession. The combination of Odegaard’s introduction, the tactical tweak and some choice words look to have done the trick.

Superb double save from the Fleetwood goalkeeper Lynch, beating away Dowman’s shot and then getting a hand to Havertz’s volley on the follow up. It was a switch of play from Odegaard to start the move, and an immaculate first touch from Dowman.

O’Neill has shown some quick feet and no shortage of skill down the left for Arsenal early in the second half, McLean is booked for a trip. Odegaard close to splitting the Fleetwood defence with a reverse pass. One-way traffic now.

They will not be hanging this one in the National Gallery, but Arsenal are level. Bright play from O’Neill down the left, putting his marker on his heels and whipping early delivery into the box. Gyokeres needed a couple of stabs at it, but the application of studs on ball was enough to sneak it beyond the goalkeeper.

Martin Odegaard has done more in five minutes than any of the 11 who were on the pitch in the first half. A class act, the best midfielder in the Premier League when he is on song.

Viktor Gyökeres gets his first goal of the season and Arsenal are level against Fleetwood! 🔴 https://t.co/LfZcIbAfCX

Arsenal camped in the Fleetwood half, but yet to carve out that clear-cut chance. When they have the ball, Hincapie, Mosquera and White are playing as a back three. Odegaard enjoying plenty of touches early in the half.

Can Arsenal shift up a gear or two in the second half? White for Timber feels pre-planned but Arteta will not have wanted to call for Odegaard at this stage.

No messing around here from Arsenal. Martin Odegaard and Ben White have both done a rigorous half-time warm up and will be introduced immediately.

Odegaard and White on, replacing Timber and Salmon. I think that means Lewis-Skelly to left-back.

Arsenal waste a corner just before half-time whistle, and they have 45 minutes to spare themselves an embarrassing League Cup exit to League Two Fleetwood Town. The home team scored with their only shot of the game, with Arsenal’s defence undone a little too easily and Marli Salmon exposed.

Since then, Arsenal have dominated possession but have not produced enough quality around the box. Still a long way to go, but a mammoth cup shock at least feels possible.

Half a chance for Jurrien Timber, but he misdirects his glancing header from Dowman’s free-kick. Dowman’s set-piece delivery has been excellent in difficult conditions.

Fleetwood enjoy a spell of territory in the Arsenal half,  Loupalo-Bi leading the line well again before Lewis-Skelly’s backpass put Meslier under some pressure.

Meslier claimed the resulting long throw well, and bowled out a quick throw to Gyokeres, but Batty sprinted back to ease out the Arsenal striker a little too easily.

There will be seven minutes of added time to play. The pattern of the game is fixed now, but Arsenal are not creating enough danger from their heaps of possession.

Hincapie whips a cross through the Fleetwood penalty area, but no Arsenal player was on the end of it in the six-yard box. We await to find out how much stoppage time there is to play.

More menace about Arsenal’s last few attacks, with Lewis-Skelly and Havertz combining and then Bennett doing ever so well to clear Dowman’s driven cross. Havertz then skews a header wide, from another Dowman delivery.

Lots of Arsenal possession without really stretching the Fleetwood defence, before Ched Evans buys a foul against Mosquera to relieve the pressure. Arteta will want the players on the pitch to figure things out, without him having to call for some big guns off the bench.

Hincapie and Mosquera have not played much Premier League football, and it is showing in their passing so far. Quality of Arsenal’s build-up from the back has been scratchy, making it easier for Fleetwood to set themselves behind the ball.

Gyokeres with a snap shot that he was always stretching for and it was simple work for the goalkeeper Lynch. Half hour gone, but we will be playing until almost 55 minutes in this first half.

Hincapie’s pass towards O’Neill goes astray. Fleetwood’s defensive shape is serving them well so far, they are defending in a 5-4-1 are limiting space. When Arsenal do lose the ball, they look open. They needed a Zubimendi interception to thwart a counter-attack after a Mosquera givaway.

Max Dowman runs out of room down the right as some rain swirls around the stadium. I’m not sure there will be any panic in the Arsenal ranks, but they need to be crisper than they have been so far.

Something of a scramble from a wide Arsenal free-kick but the home team survive and there is a huge roar from the home crowd. Lewis-Skelly then slips in midfield and Loupalo-Bi helps drag Fleetwood up the pitch.

One of the two Fleetwood players to come into the team from the defeat by Exeter has scored, Loupalo-Bi. He pinned Salmon as the last man and rolled the young Arsenal defender, before poking the ball through the legs of Meslier. Loupalo-Bi is on loan from Fulham. Is the shock of all shocks on?

Well, well, well. The stadium reeks of sulphur from the red plumes of smoke that have been set off in celebration. Whatever criticisms you have of English football, a night like this when the minnows serve it up to giants is exactly what makes the sport great. Fleetwood might not hold on but, goodness, they have given the locals something to enjoy.

FLEETWOOD TAKE THE LEAD! 😱 Loupalo-Bi puts League Two side Fleetwood ahead against Arsenal 💥 https://t.co/zTFEkCp0oL

First big chance of the game falls to Arsenal. Salmon’s pass forward deflected through to Dowman, but he scuffed the ball across goal with his right foot just in front of Gyokeres. Could he have run around the ball and curled the shot with his left? He looked to have had the time.

Arsenal starting to apply some pressure now, and the attacks are coming from their right flank through Timber and Dowman. Rooney wins a crunching 50:50 at the edge of the box to deny Lewis-Skelly a clear shot on goal. Great block.

Another throw-in for Fleetwood high up the pitch, won by Ched Evans. Fleetwood need all of the levellers they can get tonight, and you wonder if that long stoppage right from the off can be one.

The throw-in is dangerous again, but Hincapie defends well at the back post.

Fleetwood enjoying their first passages of possession, and they win a throw-in deep in the Arsenal half, Hincapie putting the ball out.

Batty is going to launch this into the box... it’s a flat and powerful long ball but Lewis-Skelly cleared after the ball was flicked on. Havertz then wins a free-kick.

According the Peter Drury in the Sky Sports commentary box, police have now located the operator of the drone and believe the situation is under control.

We go back to the free-kick Arsenal won eight-and-a-half minutes ago.

Dowman’s delivery was excellent, but Hincapie failed to win clean contact on the header.

Play is yet to resume. The referee is currently talking to Matt Lawlor and Mikel Arteta on the touchline.

And the referee has now called the players off!

#1186. Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia

International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's world championship.

A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

#1184. As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?

Droughts, floods and extreme heat are upping the pressure on delegates at the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey. Can countries move beyond pledges to concrete action?

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet."

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff."

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to agree, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels."

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements, including phaseout plans.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.

The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.

"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power which Germany and other industrialized nations rely on to shape policy to fight climate change.

Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.

When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

This article was originally written in German.

#1183. How Emile Heskey fell into a sketchy world peddling controversial drugs: From England star worth £12m to bankruptcy, unpaid tax and a bitter divorce

Published: 07:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 07:35 EST, 26 November 2026

Emile Heskey is standing in a warehouse, dressed in a black adidas tracksuit, trying to sell you a jar of curious sweet treats.

He smiles into the camera with the gentle-giant warmth that characterised his football career – but Heskey is in unfamiliar territory.

Behind him, stacked on shelf after shelf, are containers full of Supreme CBD gummies.

The man who scored in England's 5-1 thrashing of Germany in 2001, who scored 110 Premier League goals for Leicester, Liverpool, Birmingham, Wigan and Aston Villa plus seven more for his country, is, remarkably, trying to flog you an assortment of products containing cannabidiol, a legal but controversial ingredient derived from cannabis.

Today, he is promoting a tub of CBD strawberry gummies, as well as oil. If you fancy an exclusive discount, there's a special code bearing his name.

‘I swear by these products for my sleep,’ he writes in the caption on Instagram. ‘They have been fantastic for me for years now!’

Emile Heskey spends his days trying to flog controversial Supreme CBD products (Instagram: theemileheskey)

He is one of multiple former footballers promoting the products for ex-Olympic boxer Anthony Fowler - despite their illegal claims about the supposed health benefits

Heskey, 48, was once one of English football's most respected players. He won 62 caps for England, appearing at two World Cups. He won five trophies at Liverpool and two League Cups at Leicester.

Occasionally mocked for his lack of goals – he averaged roughly one every five games during his club career – he carried himself with humour and grace. Since retiring, his reputation has helped him secure roles with England's youth pathway and Leicester's women's team, as well as occasional punditry work for the BBC.

In September, he scored in an England legends match against Poland, playing alongside John Terry and Robbie Fowler. This month, he was a guest of honour at Liverpool's Anfield VIP Experience. He remains a regular on the speakers' circuit, with more appearances booked before Christmas.

All of which begs the question: what is he doing promoting Supreme CBD? Why is he filming several videos a month for a company with such a troubled regulatory record?

Where once he shared a dressing room with Steven Gerrard and David Beckham, he now shares an ambassadorial roster with Katie Price.

It is unclear whether Heskey is aware of the concerns surrounding Supreme CBD products, or the repeated occasions on which the company has fallen foul of advertising rules.

Its founder, Anthony Fowler, a former Team GB Olympic boxer, has made unsubstantiated claims that his cannabidiol products can help treat mental health conditions and autism in children.

There is likely a financial incentive for Heskey, although the terms of any arrangement are unclear. Equally, he appears genuinely convinced of the products' benefits. He claims the oil has done wonders for his sleep and eased his aches and pains.

Heskey's wife Chantelle has issued divorce proceedings - and claims he cancelled a holiday with their kids to go away with his new partner instead

Heskey and his new partner Jade Slusarczyk spent two weeks together in Cyprus and Greece

Chantelle branded Heskey 'vile' and claimed he deleted her comment on an Instagram post about the new couple's holiday

That may well be true. The NHS acknowledges that CBD has some medical uses, but warns that the ‘quality and content’ of products sold online can be uncertain and that they ‘may be illegal and potentially dangerous’. Nor is there any guarantee that products sold in health stores will be of ‘good quality’.

Supreme CBD have repeatedly breached advertising rules. In June, the Advertising Standards Authority took action over the company's continued use of prohibited claims that CBD could treat, prevent or cure human disease.

The regulator has also upheld complaints about celebrity promotions that failed to make clear they were advertisements.

Supreme CBD have made claims that their products can treat anxiety, insomnia and depression. Such medicinal claims are prohibited in advertising for products that have not been authorised as medicines. It is uncomfortable ground for Heskey to find himself on.

Last year, Fowler also spoke about refusing chemotherapy for his two-year-old daughter's tumour, claiming CBD oil had had a 'massive' effect on it instead. Price, a paid brand ambassador, amplified those claims on her own social media channels, including posted to her 1.6million followers on X that the tumour had 'shrunk' as a result.

British medical and food safety authorities advise that CBD should not be given to those under the age of 18.

CBD can also affect how other medicines work, meaning anyone using it alongside other treatments should seek medical advice. Certain medicinal CBD treatments require regular monitoring because of their potential effects on the liver.

It is not unusual for former sportspeople to struggle with insomnia, depression or persistent pain after retirement. In a digital world where anyone can extol the virtues of a product to thousands of followers, it is perhaps unsurprising that cannabis oil has attracted so much attention. Some users say it has helped them.

Heskey celebrates with David Beckham after scoring for England against Denmark at the 2002 World Cup

Many of Heskey's almost 100,000 Instagram followers appear equally enthusiastic, with comments beneath his posts endorsing the benefits he describes.

And Heskey is hardly alone among former footballers. Supreme CBD products have also been endorsed by former Arsenal and England playmaker Paul Merson – who has his name on a bundle of his 'favourite' products available to buy on the company's website – Heskey's old Liverpool team-mate Chris Kirkland, Southampton hero Matt Le Tissier and ex-Nottingham Forest goalkeeper Mark Crossley, while ex-Liverpool striker John Aldridge has insisted the product was ‘good for me’.

Life after football has, at times, been rather messy for Heskey.

In 2009, his wealth was estimated at £12million. He had built a clean-cut image and maintained a relatively low profile away from the pitch. Yet just a year later, in 2010, he was declared bankrupt.

His subsequent business dealings have brought further difficulties. Earlier this year, Heskey became caught up in a legal dispute surrounding an allegedly fraudulent £15m takeover of Cypriot club Apollon Limassol by British businessman Craig Gabriel.

Heskey had been lined up to become the face of the takeover and a club director. There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on his part.

In 2023, Heskey was found to have defaulted on £92,000 in tax relating to his work as a football development officer between 2017 and 2020. He was handed a £42,000 penalty.

That same year, a celebrity bar and restaurant he had funded, and which was overseen by his wife Chantelle, was wound up by the courts with debts totalling £163,000.

Former England footballer Heskey has found love with former Miss Blackpool Slusarczyk

Parea, which opened in 2018, had been a regular haunt of footballers and television personalities, including members of the Real Housewives of Cheshire cast. But a local catering company applied to have the business wound up over unpaid debts.

The restaurant had previously made headlines in 2019 when its first anniversary party featured sushi served on a semi-naked woman lying on a table, her modesty largely preserved by strategically placed leaves and pieces of salmon.

In 2024, Heskey faced further financial difficulties linked to his involvement in a celebrity investment scheme that became embroiled in a £1.6billion tax dispute.

The scheme was reportedly operated by Ingenious Media, a financing company that backed dozens of films. Investors were said to include Beckham, Gerrard, Jeremy Paxman, Robbie Williams and Heskey, with a minimum investment of £50,000.

Gerrard and the composer Andrew Lloyd Webber were among those who launched legal proceedings against HSBC in 2018, alleging that the bank had ‘dishonestly assisted’ Ingenious Media.

In the same year, Heskey was ordered to pay almost £200,000 in a dispute involving an unpaid £1.63m tax bill.

His personal life has also become complicated. Heskey appears to be estranged from his wife Chantelle, whom he married in 2014 and with whom he has four children. In August, she branded him ‘vile’ following a holiday he took with his new partner.

Heskey had gone public with his relationship with Jade Slusarczyk, a former Sky Sports walk-on girl accompanying darts players to the oche, in July. Within a month, the couple were holidaying in Cyprus and Greece, sharing photographs of their trip on Instagram.

Parea, a popular Cheshire bar loved by footballers and celebrities and owned by Heskey and his wife, was wound up with debts of £163,000

‘The best two weeks away with you,’ he wrote. The posts provoked an angry response from Chantelle, who has begun divorce proceedings and accused Heskey of letting his family down in comments beneath the photographs. She subsequently claimed that Heskey had deleted her comment and described him as ‘vile’.

Daily Mail Sport has contacted Mrs Heskey's representatives on multiple occasions, but they have declined to comment.

Emile and Chantelle have two sons, Reigan and Jaden, both footballers, and two younger daughters, Milanna and Mendez. Jaden made his Manchester City debut in the Carabao Cup last season and is now on loan at Sheffield Wednesday, while Reigan was sold to Cologne in the summer.

Speaking to Daily Mail Sport last year, Heskey praised his sons' athletic ability and suggested that both could one day play for England's senior team. He was happy to talk on that occasion, speaking as he helped coach children at a football camp.

This time, however, Daily Mail Sport has been met with silence. We have made repeated attempts, through multiple reporters, to put questions to Heskey about his involvement with Supreme CBD. His representatives have either declined to comment or failed to respond.

We wanted to know whether he was aware of the advertising rulings against Supreme CBD, and whether he had any concerns about the medical claims made by its founder. We would also have welcomed his account of the personal and financial difficulties described here.

And so we are left watching Heskey from afar, returning to the warehouse for video after video, smiling and cracking jokes with Fowler.

Heskey scores the fifth goal in England's 5-1 trouncing of Germany in 2001

We have made repeated attempts to put questions to Heskey about his involvement with Supreme CBD. His representatives have either declined to comment or failed to respond

‘When you find the best dose for you, there's no going back,’ he declares in the caption to one post from October.

Perched on a green sofa, encouraging his followers to buy products from a company with a deeply controversial advertising record, he seems entirely at ease.

Whether Heskey has any reservations about the business whose products he so enthusiastically promotes is something we would dearly like to know.

For now, the former England striker is still smiling for the camera.

But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

This was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

The pain of losing a player of Ngumoha’s potential does not pass quickly, especially as the winger was part of Chelsea’s academy system for eight years. It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1181. 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner said. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

"For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he said.

Eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."

Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

"I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color."

She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

#1180. Amorim: ‘Milan can defend better, were too soft in Europa League’

Ruben Amorim insists that despite a very attacking Milan line-up against Olympiacos, they can ‘defend better’ than in previous ‘soft’ Europa League performances.

It kicks off at the Stadio Georgios Karaisakis in Piraeus at 17.45 GMT (18.45 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game, Juventus-Omonia Nicosia and Borac-Atalanta on the Liveblog.

The Rossoneri absolutely must get points in Greece this evening, because they lost three of their four Europa League games so far this season, winning 4-0 away to RB Salzburg.

They make the trip without Luka Modric, Francesco Camarda, Davide Bartesaghi, Strahinja Pavlovic, Samuel Chukwueze, Matteo Gabbia, Ruben Loftus-Cheek, Alexis Saelemaekers and Pietro Terracciano.

It is an all-attack formation, with Diego Moreira, Alphadjo Cisse, Omari Hutchinson and Goncalo Ramos together.

“In football, you need to defend and attack. Aside from the characteristics of the players, we need to attack with 11 and defend with 11,” Amorim told Sky Sport Italia.

“The players know the positions that we want on the pitch, we are ready to play and must be more compact compared to the matches against Benfica and Ferencvaros. Even with these players, who are more attacking in their characteristics, we can defend better.”

Milan have never won away to a Greek side in Europe, managing just four draws and two defeats, including a 3-1 loss to Olympiacos in December 2018.

It is notable that they have been unable to be consistent with two games in a week, so does Amorim see the right attitude today?

“I think they understood, we watched the videos, we are improving as a team. We were a little soft against Ferencvaros because we were not compact, we need to really focus on the details, when the position makes all the difference two metres one way or another.

“We did it several times in Serie A, now we need to do it in the Europa League too.”

Olympiacos can boast several former Serie A players, as Lorenzo Pirola was an Inter youth product, Remo Freuler spent time with Bologna and Atalanta, while Marcus Pedersen played for Torino.

“We need to be a good team, and to do that, we must be able to win in Serie A and in Europe. We have that responsibility, as we always say, the present is important, but we are in a long-term project. We need to know if we are ready and today is another important test for us to win,” concluded Amorim.

This is pathetic and deeply embarrassing if Milan crash out of Europe tonight. The coach must leave then.

Attacking line-up but can’t get past the halfway line. Another disgusting performance in Europe so far.

#1179. Augmenting reality with integrated photonics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 915–926 (2026) Cite this article

Augmented-reality (AR) glasses promise to transform how we interact with the world by seamlessly blending digital content with our physical surroundings. Yet making them viable for comfortable, all-day use remains deeply challenging, constrained by hard trade-offs of size, power and display performance. This calls for fundamentally new ways to generate and control light with high precision in an ultracompact form factor. Here we examine how integrated photonics can help bridge the technology gap in AR hardware. We review the basics of AR displays and recent advances in integrated photonics for new AR display components and architectures, then turn to key challenges and future directions, from component development to system innovation and scalable manufacturing, and highlight broader opportunities for synergy with fields such as quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

#1178. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.
